Chapter 5: The Problem With “Neurosexism” in Science and Society
Picture this: a busy research lab, filled with the hum of computers and the quiet focus of scientists studying brain scans. The data they’re looking at is interesting, but it’s not as black-and-white as they might’ve hoped. Sure, there are some small differences between the male and female participants, but when you really look closely, there’s a whole lot of overlap.
Yet, when the study gets written up and sent out for publication, what gets all the attention? The differences—not the similarities. Suddenly, the story becomes one of two distinct, hardwired brains: one male, one female.
This way of seeing things even has a name—“neurosexism.” It’s when neuroscience gets used to prop up old-school ideas about what men and women can or can’t do. Most of the time, it’s not even intentional. It’s more about unconscious bias—the same cultural influences that affect all of us, even in the lab.
Now, here’s something to really pay attention to: neurosexism gives old prejudices a scientific glow-up. If someone hears that “science has proven” men are naturally better at certain things, or women at others, it starts to feel like inequality is just the way things are. It suddenly seems normal that there aren’t many women in tech, or men in caregiving jobs, as if that’s just nature’s plan.
But real life—and real science—is way more complicated. The brain isn’t a fixed machine; it’s constantly shaped by our experiences, our environment, and the opportunities we’re given. A lot of the differences that show up in adults might actually come from years of being steered in certain directions, not from some kind of “hardwiring.” When scientists take things like education, encouragement, and access into account, those supposed gender differences often shrink or vanish.
The way research gets talked about matters, too. Journalists—hoping for a catchy headline—might exaggerate or oversimplify what the studies actually show. A little difference in brain activity suddenly turns into a viral story about the “male brain” or “female brain,” fueling old stereotypes. Before you know it, those stories are everywhere: in books, on talk shows, even in classrooms. And they stick around, shaping how people think in ways that can be really tough to unlearn.
Neurosexism doesn’t just change how we see others; it changes how we see ourselves. If women keep hearing that their brains aren’t cut out for science or leadership, it’s easy to start doubting their own abilities. And men can feel boxed in too, pressured to fit a certain mold of what’s “masculine.” In the end, it means a lot of talent gets wasted, and a lot of dreams get set aside.
So, how do we push back against neurosexism? It starts with asking better questions—looking past easy answers and really digging into how research is done and shared. It’s about seeing how culture shapes both science and society, and not being afraid to challenge the stories we’ve always heard.
The journey toward equality isn’t just about changing laws—it’s about changing the way we think. When we understand how gender gets constructed—not just out in the world, but also inside the lab—it opens up the possibility for something better. Imagine a future where everyone gets to follow their interests and chase their potential, free from the weight of outdated beliefs.
